messages:
ashley: Quick sync — we need to pick an egress strategy for private control plane traffic from tenant dataplanes to external services (S3, model registries, vendor APIs). Two main patterns on the table: 1) per-tenant SNAT (NAT44) with dedicated egress IPs, 2) preserve source IP via a proxy/relay and use per-tenant ENIs/IPs. Looking for tradeoffs and a recommended default.

miguel: Per-tenant SNAT is operationally simpler initially. You map tenant subnet -> public IP, advertise that IP, and upstreams see a stable client IP. Downside: IP inventory + ENI limits, and it obliterates original client IP for audits.

priya: Proxy/relay preserves source ip (if we route correctly) and keeps auditing, but adds another hop and stateful components. We need to decide where TLS terminates — at proxy or be passed through (mTLS passthrough is harder).

jordan: There's also shared-SNAT + header approach: use a shared pool but inject X-Forwarded-For / X-Redwood-Tenant headers for logging. Cheap but will fail compliance customers and any upstreams that rely on source IP for allowlists.

sam: Ops POV: per-tenant IPs means IP mgmt and potential exhaustion. Also EC2 ENI/IP quotas per instance can force us to scale horizontally. For large numbers of tenants the allocator becomes non-trivial. Hairpinning is another edge case — control plane callbacks to tenant services may need NAT back.

ashley: @sam can you run rough numbers for 200 tenants (avg) with 2 IPs each and call out where we hit ENI limits? Also how disruptive is hairpin for control plane -> tenant callbacks?

sam: Quick calc: 200 tenants * 2 IPs = 400 egress IPs. That's fine at VPC level, but per-host ENI limits vary by instance type (t3.medium ~ 2 ENIs, m5.large ~ 3-4, etc). If we pin IPs to nodes we need more nodes or use a separate egress fleet with larger instances. Hairpin: if control plane sits in same VPC and wants to hit tenant private endpoints via the same egress path, we either need return routes or SNAT for internal callbacks.

miguel: Security/regulatory: some customers insist on fixed, auditable egress IPs and will reject any header-based auditing. For them per-tenant SNAT or dedicated egress proxies with fixed IPs are required.

priya: Latency: a proxy/relay adds measurable P95 latency — ballpark 5-15ms depending on infra. For inference hot paths that matters; for control plane (webhooks, registries) it's usually fine. We should categorize flows: latency-sensitive dataplane tokens vs control-plane metadata calls.

jordan: Implementation notes: per-tenant SNAT can be implemented with iptables rules on egress nodes. Example rule we used in a spike: 
```
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.42.32.0/24 -j SNAT --to-source 198.51.100.23
```
Easy to automate but harder to reason about at scale.

ashley: Cost question — which is cheaper steady-state: maintaining NAT instances vs running proxy tasks (Fargate/ECS)?

sam: Proxy tasks = CPU/memory cost per request, autoscaling needs. NAT is lightweight per-packet CPU but requires us to manage the fleet. For high throughput, NAT on cheap instances likely cheaper. For unpredictable traffic, proxy autoscaling is more flexible. Also consider egress bandwidth pricing on cloud provider.

miguel: Proposal: hybrid default. Use a shared SNAT pool for most tenants (cheap, simple), and offer per-tenant dedicated egress IPs (SNAT or proxy) as an opt-in (enterprise/Dedicated customers). For control plane callbacks that require source preservation, run a dedicated mTLS relay that terminates/forwards identity while keeping a fixed egress IP.

priya: +1 hybrid. Also add a migration path: customers can request a dedicated IP; operator flips a flag, egress-operator assigns IP(s) and reapplies iptables / proxy config.

jordan: Operationally we should add an egress-operator API: allocate_ip(tenant), release_ip(tenant), list_allocations(). It must emit events for audit. Also add healthchecks so we know if a tenant's dedicated IPs are exhausted or misrouted.

ashley: Action items: 
- @sam: spike with instance sizing / ENI limits & cost for 200/1000 tenant scenarios (due next Tue).
- @miguel: draft egress-operator API + RBAC model.
- @priya: perf test a simple proxy relay and measure P95 for control-plane calls vs baseline.
I'll draft an RFC reflecting hybrid approach and include fallback semantics (shared->dedicated) and hairpin handling.

ops-bot: Deploy check — branch pushed: github.com/redwood/egress-operator/spike (build passed) :white_check_mark:

ashley: Thanks all, will start RFC PR and link the spike results when available.
